questions.q: A 0°/45°/90° strain rosette reads ε_0, ε_45 and ε_90. The engineering shear strain γ_xy is:
questions.x: The 45° gauge reads ε_45 = (ε_x + ε_y)/2 + γ_xy/2, so γ_xy = 2ε_45 − ε_0 − ε_90.

questions.q: A 0°/45°/90° rosette reads ε_0 = 600, ε_45 = 450 and ε_90 = −200 microstrain. Engineering shear strain γ_xy (microstrain)?
In Voigt notation, the three shear entries of the strain vector are:
w: Half the tensor shear strains, ε_ij/2
questions.x: Voigt ordering is (ε_11, ε_22, ε_33, 2ε_23, 2ε_13, 2ε_12), and the factor 2 keeps σ·ε equal to the work σ:ε.

questions.q: Finite simple shear by amount γ. The in-plane principal stretches λ₁ > λ₂ satisfy:
questions.x: Simple shear is isochoric, so λ₁λ₂ = 1, and λ₁ = γ/2 + √(1 + γ²/4), λ₂ = −γ/2 + √(1 + γ²/4) differ by exactly γ.

questions.q: Complete the Green-Lagrange strain of a fiber with reference unit direction N and stretch λ
questions.x: Since λ² = N·CN and E = ½(C − I), the fiber Green strain is ½(λ² − 1), which reduces to the small strain λ − 1 for λ near 1.

questions.q: In small strain theory, the volumetric strain dv/dV − 1 is approximately:
questions.x: J = det(I + ∇u) ≈ 1 + tr ∇u = 1 + tr ε to first order, so the volume change is the sum of the normal strains.

questions.q: Match each homogeneous motion to its deformation gradient
questions.x: A rotation is orthogonal with det 1, a dilation scales every direction equally, simple shear adds an off-diagonal γ with J = 1, and uniaxial stretch scales one axis.

questions.q: Physical meaning of the small strain component ε_12:
questions.a: Half the decrease in angle between fibers along e₁ and e₂
w: The full decrease in angle between fibers along e₁ and e₂
The rotation of the element about e₃
The stretch of the fiber along e₁ + e₂
questions.x: The engineering shear strain γ_12 = 2ε_12 equals the decrease in the right angle between fibers along e₁ and e₂.

questions.q: At a point on a traction free surface with outward unit normal n:
questions.a: σn = 0, so n is a principal direction with zero principal stress
w: Only the shear stresses on that plane are zero, the normal stress is arbitrary
questions.x: Cauchy's theorem gives t = σn = 0 on the surface, so n is an eigenvector of σ with eigenvalue zero, while the stresses acting within the surface plane may take any value.

questions.q: σ = [[50,30,0],[30,−30,0],[0,0,20]] MPa. Magnitude of the shear traction on the plane with n = (0.6, 0.8, 0) (MPa, 1 decimal)?
Under a rotation of the coordinate axes, which quantity stays the same?
questions.x: The trace is the first invariant I₁, so the mean stress I₁/3 is the same in every coordinate frame.

questions.q: Plane stress. The planes of maximum in-plane shear carry normal stress equal to:
questions.x: Those planes sit at 45° to the principal planes, at the top and bottom of Mohr's circle, where the normal stress equals the center (σ₁ + σ₂)/2.

questions.q: Complete the plane stress transformation, θ counterclockwise from x
questions.x: σ_x' = σ_x cos²θ + σ_y sin²θ + 2τ_xy sinθ cosθ, and the double angle forms give the τ_xy sin 2θ term.

questions.q: In the Cauchy tetrahedron argument, why do body force and inertia drop out as the tetrahedron shrinks?
questions.a: They scale with volume, h³, while traction terms scale with area, h²
w: Body force is zero inside a solid
Inertia cancels the body force exactly
The tetrahedron is assumed to be in static equilibrium
questions.x: Dividing the force balance by the face area and letting h → 0 leaves only the surface tractions, which gives t = σn.

questions.q: Put the steps for a traction boundary condition on an inclined face in order
steps: Find the outward unit normal n of the face
Write the traction t = σn in components
Set each component equal to the applied traction
Solve for the unknown stresses or constants
questions.x: Traction conditions on an inclined face are vector conditions on t = σn, imposed component by component.

questions.q: Match each stress invariant to its form in principal stresses
questions.x: I₁, I₂ and I₃ are the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial, and J₂ = ½ s:s is the deviatoric invariant behind von Mises.

questions.q: Admissible range of Poisson's ratio for a stable isotropic linear elastic solid:
questions.x: Positive G requires ν > −1 and positive K requires ν < ½, and auxetic materials with ν < 0 sit inside that range.

questions.q: Confined compression (uniaxial strain), E = 70 GPa and ν = 0.30. Constrained modulus M = σ_11/ε_11 (GPa, 1 decimal)?
The major symmetry C_ijkl = C_klij of the stiffness tensor follows from:
questions.a: Existence of a strain energy density W(ε)
questions.x: With σ_ij = ∂W/∂ε_ij, C_ijkl = ∂²W/∂ε_ij∂ε_kl, and equality of mixed partial derivatives gives C_ijkl = C_klij.

questions.q: The isotropic strain energy is positive definite exactly when:
questions.x: Splitting strain into volumetric and deviatoric parts gives W = (K/2)(tr ε)² + μ e:e, so positivity requires μ > 0 and K = λ + 2μ/3 > 0.

questions.q: Complete the first Lamé constant in terms of E and ν
questions.x: λ = Eν/((1 + ν)(1 − 2ν)), which grows toward infinity as ν approaches ½.

questions.q: A linear elastic bar under uniaxial stress σ. Its volumetric strain is:
questions.x: The axial strain σ/E plus two lateral strains −νσ/E sum to σ(1 − 2ν)/E, which equals σ/(3K).

questions.q: For an isotropic linear elastic solid, the principal directions of σ and ε:
questions.x: σ = λ tr(ε) I + 2μ ε is a sum of ε and a multiple of I, so σ and ε share eigenvectors.

questions.q: Match each elastic modulus to the test that measures it directly
questions.x: E = σ/ε under uniaxial stress, G = τ/γ in shear, K = −p/ε_v under pressure, and M = λ + 2μ when the lateral strains are held at zero.

questions.q: Plane stress, isotropic linear elastic. The out-of-plane strain ε_33 is:
questions.x: With σ_33 = 0, Hooke's law gives ε_33 = −(ν/E)(σ_11 + σ_22), so a thin plate thins under in-plane tension.

questions.q: A small circular hole in a fuselage skin with remote hoop stress 80 MPa and axial stress 40 MPa. Peak hoop stress at the hole edge (MPa)?
questions.x: Superposed Kirsch solutions give σ_θθ = (σ₁ + σ₂) − 2(σ₁ − σ₂)cos 2θ, peaking at 3σ₁ − σ₂ = 240 − 40 = 200 MPa.

questions.q: To convert a plane stress solution into the plane strain solution, replace:
questions.a: E by E/(1 − ν²) and ν by ν/(1 − ν)
w: E by E(1 − ν²) and ν by ν(1 − ν)
E by E/(1 − ν) and ν by ν/(1 + ν)
ν by ν/(1 + ν) and keep E
questions.x: Eliminating σ_33 = ν(σ_11 + σ_22) from the plane strain Hooke's law gives a law of the plane stress form with effective constants E/(1 − ν²) and ν/(1 − ν).

questions.q: The Airy function φ = Ay³ represents:
questions.x: σ_11 = φ,yy = 6Ay is linear through the depth while σ_22 = φ,xx and σ_12 = −φ,xy vanish, which is pure bending.

questions.q: Complete the polar Airy hoop stress
questions.x: In polar form σ_θθ = ∂²φ/∂r², while σ_rr = (1/r)φ,r + (1/r²)φ,θθ and σ_rθ = −∂/∂r((1/r)φ,θ).

questions.q: A small circular hole in a large plate under pure shear (σ₁ = τ, σ₂ = −τ). Peak hoop stress magnitude at the hole edge:
questions.x: σ_θθ = (σ₁ + σ₂) − 2(σ₁ − σ₂)cos 2θ = −4τ cos 2θ, so the edge reaches ±4τ.

questions.q: Put the steps of the Airy stress function method in order
steps: Choose φ with ∇⁴φ = 0 matching the polynomial form of the load
Compute σ_11 = φ,yy, σ_22 = φ,xx, σ_12 = −φ,xy
Impose pointwise traction conditions on the long edges
Impose force and moment resultants at the ends (Saint-Venant) to fix the remaining constants
Find strains from Hooke's law and integrate for displacements
questions.x: The biharmonic φ secures equilibrium and compatibility, strong conditions fix the long edges, resultants fix the ends, and displacements come last.

questions.q: The axisymmetric Airy function φ = A ln r + Br² gives:
w: σ_rr = A ln r + B, σ_θθ = A/r + 2Br
questions.x: σ_rr = (1/r)dφ/dr = A/r² + 2B and σ_θθ = d²φ/dr² = −A/r² + 2B, which is the Lamé form.

questions.q: Same p, R and allowable stress. Thin sphere wall thickness compared with a thin cylinder:
questions.x: The sphere membrane stress is pR/(2t) against the cylinder hoop stress pR/t, so the sphere needs half the wall.

questions.q: Solid steel disc in plane stress, ρ = 7800 kg/m³, ν = 0.3, outer radius b = 0.5 m, spinning at ω = 200 rad/s. Centre stress σ_rr = σ_θθ = (3 + ν)ρω²b²/8 (MPa, 2 decimals)?
questions.x: (3.3/8)(7800)(200²)(0.5²) = 32.18 MPa, equibiaxial at the centre.

questions.q: A tiny central bore is drilled in a spinning solid disc. The peak hoop stress:
questions.a: Roughly doubles, to (3 + ν)ρω²b²/4 at the bore
w: Stays at the solid disc centre value
Drops to zero at the bore
questions.x: The traction free bore forces σ_rr = 0 there, and the hoop stress at a vanishing bore tends to twice the solid disc centre value.

questions.q: Thin-wall vessel formulas are accurate when:
w: p is below the yield stress
questions.x: For t/R ≤ 0.1 the hoop stress is nearly uniform through the wall and pR/t agrees with Lamé to within a few percent.

questions.q: Complete the radial growth of a thin sphere under internal pressure
questions.x: Equibiaxial membrane stress pR/(2t) gives ε_θ = (1 − ν)pR/(2Et), and Δr = Rε_θ.

questions.q: Thick cylinder, inner radius a, outer radius b, loaded by external pressure p only. Bore hoop stress?
questions.x: With σ_rr(a) = 0 and σ_rr(b) = −p, A = −pb²/(b² − a²) and σ_θθ(a) = 2A, the largest compressive hoop stress.

questions.q: Autofrettage of a gun barrel works by:
questions.a: Overpressure yields the inner wall, leaving residual hoop compression at the bore
w: Heat treating the bore to raise yield strength
Adding a second shell with an interference fit
Thinning the wall so stress is uniform
questions.x: After the plastic overload is removed, the elastic outer wall squeezes the yielded bore, and that residual compression offsets the service hoop tension.

questions.q: Put the steps of the Lamé thick cylinder solution in order
steps: Write radial equilibrium dσ_rr/dr + (σ_rr − σ_θθ)/r = 0
Insert Hooke's law with ε_rr = du/dr and ε_θθ = u/r
Solve the Euler equation for u = C₁r + C₂/r
Apply σ_rr(a) = −p_i and σ_rr(b) = −p_o
questions.x: Equilibrium plus Hooke's law plus kinematics gives a displacement ODE whose solution C₁r + C₂/r is fixed by the two radial traction conditions.

questions.q: Objectivity requires a hyperelastic strain energy W(F) to depend on F:
w: Only through B = FFᵀ, for any material
questions.x: W(QF) = W(F) for every rotation Q, and choosing Q = Rᵀ shows W depends on U, hence on C = U².

questions.q: Incompressible neo-Hookean bar, μ = 0.4 MPa, uniaxial stretch λ = 1.5. Nominal (first Piola) stress P_11 (MPa, 3 decimals)?
In incompressible hyperelasticity, the pressure p in σ = −pI + 2B ∂W/∂B plays the role of:
w: A material constant fitted from tests
The bulk modulus times tr E
questions.x: The constraint J = 1 makes p a reaction, determined by equilibrium and the traction boundary conditions.

questions.q: Universal relation for simple shear by γ of any isotropic elastic solid:
questions.x: The relation holds for every isotropic constitutive law, and the neo-Hookean values μγ² and μγ satisfy it.

questions.q: Complete the thin Mooney-Rivlin balloon pressure (H = undeformed thickness, R = undeformed radius)
questions.x: The C₂ term adds a factor (1 + (C₂/C₁)λ²), and C₂ = 0 with C₁ = μ/2 recovers the neo-Hookean (2μH/R)(λ⁻¹ − λ⁻⁷).

questions.q: A Mooney-Rivlin balloon with C₂/C₁ large enough is inflated. Pressure versus stretch shows:
questions.a: A peak, a valley, then rising pressure, so inflation snaps to a larger radius
w: A single peak, then decay to zero
A monotonic rise from the start
A constant plateau after the peak
questions.x: The (C₂/C₁)λ² factor stiffens the skin at large stretch, so pressure climbs again after the valley and the balloon jumps between branches at equal pressure.

questions.q: Put the thin incompressible balloon setup in order
steps: Set λ_θ = λ_φ = λ = R/R₀ and λ_r = λ⁻² from J = 1
Use σ_rr ≈ 0 through the thin wall to fix the pressure multiplier
Find σ_θθ = μ(λ² − λ⁻⁴) from σ = −pI + μB
Balance a hemisphere, PπR² = σ_θθ 2πR t, with t = t₀λ⁻²
questions.x: Incompressibility fixes the thickness stretch, the free thin wall fixes the multiplier, and hemisphere equilibrium gives P = 2μ(t₀/R₀)(λ⁻¹ − λ⁻⁷).

questions.q: Match each hyperelastic model to its strain energy
questions.x: Neo-Hookean and Mooney-Rivlin use invariants of B, Saint Venant-Kirchhoff carries Hooke's law over to the Green strain E, and Ogden works directly in principal stretches.

questions.q: In the Eulerian (spatial) description, field quantities are functions of:
questions.a: Current position x and time t
w: Reference position X and time t
questions.x: The spatial description watches fixed points in space, so fields are written φ(x, t) and particles pass through them.

questions.q: 1D spatial velocity v = 2t x (m/s, x in m, t in s). Particle acceleration at x = 1.5 m, t = 0.5 s (m/s²)?
Which statement expresses an isochoric motion in rate form?
questions.x: J̇ = J div v, so J stays at 1 when div v = tr D = 0 at every point.

questions.q: Conservation of mass in the referential (Lagrangian) form:
questions.x: The mass ρ dv = ρJ dV of each element equals its reference mass ρ₀ dV, so ρJ = ρ₀.

questions.q: Complete the spatial acceleration, with (∇v)_ij = ∂v_i/∂x_j
questions.x: In index form a_i = ∂v_i/∂t + v_i,j v_j, the local plus convective acceleration.

questions.q: Passing from a global balance ∫_Ω f dv = 0 to the local form f = 0 uses:
w: Ω equal to the whole body
questions.x: If the integral vanishes for every subregion and f is continuous, f vanishes at every point (localization).

questions.q: Steady velocity field (∂v/∂t = 0) through a converging duct. The particle acceleration is:
w: Zero, since the flow is steady
questions.x: Particles speed up as they move into the narrower section, and the convective term (∇v)v captures that change along their paths.

questions.q: Match each balance law to its local spatial form
questions.x: Continuity, Cauchy's equation of motion, stress symmetry and the first law are the four local balance statements in the current configuration.

questions.q: An isotropic block fully restrained in all three directions is heated by ΔT. Its stress is:
questions.x: Zero total strain gives σ(1 − 2ν)/E + αΔT = 0, so σ = −EαΔT/(1 − 2ν) = −3KαΔT, hydrostatic.

questions.q: Unidirectional glass/epoxy, V_f = 0.5, E_f = 72 GPa, α_f = 5 × 10⁻⁶ /K, E_m = 3.5 GPa, α_m = 60 × 10⁻⁶ /K. Longitudinal α₁ in 10⁻⁶ /K (2 decimals)?
questions.x: α₁ = (E_fα_fV_f + E_mα_mV_m)/(E_fV_f + E_mV_m) = (180 + 105)/(36 + 1.75) = 7.55 × 10⁻⁶ /K, close to the fiber value.

questions.q: A thick cylinder with a hot bore in steady radial conduction. The thermal hoop stress is:
questions.a: Compressive at the hot bore and tensile at the cooler outer wall
w: Tensile at the hot bore and compressive at the outer wall
Zero, since the cylinder is free to expand
questions.x: The hot inner material is held back by the cooler outer wall, so the bore is squeezed in hoop compression and the outer wall is stretched.

questions.q: A free thin plate has a linear through-thickness temperature profile. Its thermal stresses are:
questions.a: Zero, as the plate bends freely into a spherical cap
questions.x: A linear thermal strain matches ε = ε⁰ + zκ exactly, so a free plate accommodates it by curvature and stays stress free.

questions.q: Complete isotropic thermoelastic Hooke's law
questions.x: The free thermal strain αΔT I is an equal expansion in every direction, added to the mechanical strain.

questions.q: How many independent elastic constants describe an orthotropic ply in plane stress?
questions.x: Reciprocity ν₂₁/E₂ = ν₁₂/E₁ ties ν₂₁ to the others, leaving E₁, E₂, ν₁₂ and G₁₂.

questions.q: A unidirectional carbon/epoxy ply is pulled at 45° to its fibers. Its axial stiffness is governed mostly by:
questions.a: G₁₂ and E₂, the matrix dominated terms
questions.x: 1/E_45 = ¼(1/E₁ + 1/E₂ + 1/G₁₂ − 2ν₁₂/E₁), and the large compliances 1/G₁₂ and 1/E₂ dominate the sum.

questions.q: Put the steps for thermal stress in a two-material assembly (bolt in a sleeve) in order
steps: Let each part expand freely by αΔT L
Write equilibrium: one force F, tension in the bolt and equal compression in the sleeve
Write compatibility in terms of F: the free length mismatch equals the sum of the elastic changes FL/(EA) of both parts
Solve for F, then each stress F/A
questions.x: Free expansion sets the mismatch, equilibrium leaves a single unknown force F, compatibility shares the mismatch between the parts through their flexibilities L/(EA), and F divided by each area gives the stresses.
